title: There Is No One Left
paragraphs: Everyone said that Mary Lennox was the most disagreeable-looking child they had ever seen. They said it when she was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle, and it was true. She had a thin little face and a thin little body, with thin, light hair and a sour look. Her hair was yellow, and so was her face, because she had been born in India and had always been sick with one thing or another. Her father had worked for the English Government and had always been busy and unwell himself. Her mother had been a great beauty who cared only about going to parties and having fun with cheerful people. She had not wanted a little girl at all. When Mary was born, she handed her over to an Ayah, who was made to understand that if she wanted to please the Mem Sahib, she must keep the child out of sight as much as she could. So when Mary was a sickly, fussy, ugly baby, she was kept out of the way. When she grew into a sickly, fussy toddler, she was kept out of the way too. The only faces she ever remembered seeing every day were the dark faces of her Ayah and the other native servants. They always obeyed her and let her have her own way in everything, because the Mem Sahib would be angry if her crying disturbed her. So by the time Mary was six years old, she was as bossy and selfish a little pig as ever lived. The young English governess who came to teach her to read and write disliked her so much that she quit after three months. When other governesses came to fill the job, they always left even sooner than the first. So if Mary had not decided that she really wanted to learn to read books, she would never have learned her letters at all.
One terribly hot morning, when she was about nine years old, she woke up feeling very cross. She became even crosser when she saw that the servant standing by her bed was not her Ayah.
“Why did you come?” she said to the strange woman. “I won’t let you stay. Send my Ayah to me.”

The woman looked frightened, but all she could do was stammer that the Ayah could not come. When Mary flew into a rage and hit and kicked her, the woman only looked more frightened and repeated that it was not possible for the Ayah to come to Missie Sahib.

There was something mysterious in the air that morning. Nothing was done in its usual order, and several of the native servants seemed to be missing. The ones Mary did see crept or hurried about with gray, scared faces. But no one would tell her anything, and her Ayah did not come. As the morning went on, she was left completely alone. At last she wandered out into the garden and began to play by herself under a tree near the veranda. She pretended she was making a flower bed, and she stuck big scarlet hibiscus blossoms into little heaps of earth. All the while she grew angrier and angrier, muttering to herself the things she would say and the names she would call Saidie when she came back.
“Pig! Pig! Daughter of Pigs!” she said, because to call a native a pig is the worst insult of all.

She was grinding her teeth and saying this over and over when she heard her mother come out onto the veranda with someone. It was a fair young man, and they stood talking together in low, strange voices. Mary knew the fair young man, who looked like a boy. She had heard that he was a very young officer who had just come from England. The child stared at him, but she stared most at her mother. She always did this when she had the chance to see her, because the Mem Sahib (Mary called her that more often than anything else) was such a tall, slim, pretty person and wore such lovely clothes. Her hair was like curly silk, and she had a delicate little nose that seemed to look down on things, and large, laughing eyes. All her clothes were thin and floaty, and Mary said they were “full of lace.” They looked even fuller of lace than ever this morning, but her eyes were not laughing at all. They were large and scared, and they were lifted pleadingly to the face of the fair boy officer.
“Is it really so bad? Oh, is it?” Mary heard her say.
“Dreadful,” the young man answered in a shaking voice. “Dreadful, Mrs. Lennox. You should have gone to the hills two weeks ago.”
The Mem Sahib wrung her hands.
“Oh, I know I should have!” she cried. “I only stayed to go to that silly dinner party. What a fool I was!”

At that very moment, such a loud wailing broke out from the servants’ quarters that she clutched the young man’s arm, and Mary stood shivering from head to foot. The wailing grew wilder and wilder. “What is it? What is it?” Mrs. Lennox gasped.
“Someone has died,” answered the boy officer. “You didn’t tell me it had broken out among your servants.”
“I didn’t know!” the Mem Sahib cried. “Come with me! Come with me!” And she turned and ran into the house.

After that, terrible things happened, and the mystery of the morning was explained to Mary. The cholera had broken out in its deadliest form, and people were dying like flies. The Ayah had fallen ill in the night, and the servants had wailed in the huts because she had just died. Before the next day, three other servants were dead, and others had run away in terror. There was panic on every side, and there were dying people in all the bungalows.

During the confusion and bewilderment of the second day, Mary hid in the nursery, and everyone forgot about her. Nobody thought of her, nobody wanted her, and strange things happened that she knew nothing about. Mary cried and slept by turns through the hours. She only knew that people were sick and that she kept hearing mysterious, frightening sounds. Once she crept into the dining room and found it empty. A half-finished meal was still on the table, and the chairs and plates looked as if they had been shoved back in a hurry when the diners suddenly got up for some reason. The child ate some fruit and biscuits, and because she was thirsty, she drank a glass of wine that stood almost full. It was sweet, and she did not know how strong it was. Very soon it made her terribly drowsy. She went back to her nursery and shut herself in again, frightened by the cries she heard in the huts and the hurrying sound of feet. The wine made her so sleepy that she could hardly keep her eyes open. She lay down on her bed and knew nothing more for a long time.
Many things happened during the hours when she slept so heavily. But she was not disturbed by the wailing or by the sound of things being carried in and out of the bungalow.

When she woke up, she lay there and stared at the wall. The house was perfectly still. She had never known it to be so quiet before. She heard no voices and no footsteps, and she wondered if everybody had recovered from the cholera and the trouble was over. She also wondered who would take care of her now that her Ayah was dead. There would be a new Ayah, and perhaps she would know some new stories. Mary had grown rather tired of the old ones. She did not cry because her nurse had died. She was not an affectionate child and had never cared much for anyone. The noise and rushing about and wailing over the cholera had frightened her, and she had been angry because no one seemed to remember she was alive. Everyone was too panicked to think of a little girl nobody was fond of. When people had the cholera, it seemed they remembered nothing but themselves. But if everyone had gotten well again, surely someone would remember her and come looking for her.

But no one came, and as she lay waiting, the house seemed to grow quieter and quieter. She heard something rustling on the matting, and when she looked down, she saw a little snake gliding along and watching her with eyes like jewels. She was not frightened, because he was a harmless little thing that would not hurt her, and he seemed to be in a hurry to get out of the room. He slipped under the door as she watched him.
“How strange and quiet it is,” she said. “It sounds as if there is no one in the bungalow but me and the snake.”

Almost the next minute, she heard footsteps in the compound, and then on the veranda. They were men’s footsteps, and the men came into the bungalow and talked in low voices. No one went to meet them or speak to them, and they seemed to be opening doors and looking into rooms.
“What a sad, empty place!” she heard one voice say. “That pretty, pretty woman! I suppose the child, too. I heard there was a child, though no one ever saw her.”

Mary was standing in the middle of the nursery when they opened the door a few minutes later. She looked like an ugly, cross little thing, and she was frowning because she was starting to feel hungry and shamefully neglected. The first man to come in was a large officer she had once seen talking to her father. He looked tired and troubled, but when he saw her he was so startled that he almost jumped back.
“Barney!” he cried out. “There is a child here! A child alone! In a place like this! Heaven help us, who is she?”

“I am Mary Lennox,” the little girl said, drawing herself up stiffly. She thought the man was very rude to call her father’s bungalow “a place like this!” “I fell asleep when everyone had the cholera, and I only just woke up. Why does nobody come?”
“It’s the child no one ever saw!” exclaimed the man, turning to his companions. “She has actually been forgotten!”
“Why was I forgotten?” Mary said, stamping her foot. “Why does nobody come?”
The young man named Barney looked at her with great sadness. Mary even thought she saw him blink, as if he were blinking away tears.
“Poor little kid!” he said. “There is nobody left to come.”

That was the strange and sudden way Mary found out that she had neither father nor mother left. They had died and been carried away in the night. The few native servants who had not died had also left the house as fast as they could get out of it, and not one of them had remembered that there was a Missie Sahib. That was why the place was so quiet. It was true that there was no one in the bungalow but herself and the little rustling snake.
